The words

Jesus, the very thought of Thee
With sweetness fills the breast;
But sweeter far Thy face to see,
And in Thy presence rest.

Nor voice can sing, nor heart can frame,
Nor can the memory find
A sweeter sound than Thy blest name,
O Savior of mankind!

O hope of every contrite heart,
O joy of all the meek,
To those who fall, how kind Thou art!
How good to those who seek!

But what to those who find? Ah, this
Nor tongue nor pen can show;
The love of Jesus, what it is,
None but His loved ones know.

Jesus, our only joy be Thou,
As Thou our prize will be;
Jesus be Thou our glory now,
And through eternity.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum G and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on m (B).
  • Count the time. 3/4 means three crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Edward Caswall’s translation of the Latin hymn Jesu dulcis memoria, attributed to Bernard of Clairvaux, was published in Lyra Catholica in 1849. The tune ST. AGNES is by John Bacchus Dykes (1866).

  • Words: Jesu dulcis memoria (Latin, 12th century)
  • Translated (1849): Edward Caswall (1814–1878)
  • Music (1866): John Bacchus Dykes (1823–1876)

Melody from the Open Hymnal Project (public domain), edited by Brian J. Dumont; tune ST. Questions about Jesus, the Very Thought of Thee

What is the doh of Jesus, the Very Thought of Thee?

In this version, in G major, doh is G. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Jesus, the Very Thought of Thee start on?

It starts on m (B in G major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to m.

Is Jesus, the Very Thought of Thee in the public domain?

Yes. Edward Caswall died in 1878, John Bacchus Dykes died in 1876; the words were first published in 1849 and the music in 1866. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
